title: Jackie the Eagle Delivers a 'Dramatic Slap' to Nocturnal Nest Intruder
summary: In the wee hours of May 31, viewers of the Big Bear eagle nest livestream witnessed a moment of pure parental instinct. Jackie, the matriarch of a beloved bald eagle pair, was jolted from sleep by Fiona, a San Bernardino flying squirrel that had crept too close. Jackie's response was swift and unambiguous: a forceful wing-slap and a series of sharp vocalizations that the nonprofit Friends of Big Bear Valley (FOBBV) described as 'backtalk.' The message was clear—tolerating a bushy-tailed rodent while trying to sleep was not on the agenda. Fiona is one of several flying squirrels that inhabit the pine tree overlooking Big Bear Lake. These nocturnal gliders, a subspecies of Humboldt's flying squirrel, can soar up to 300 feet between trees and often scavenge the nest for fish tails, eggshells, and crunchy beetles. While they pose no serious threat to the eaglets, Jackie's vigilance is understandable. This nesting season has been a roller coaster. In January, ravens destroyed the pair's first two eggs. Jackie and Shadow laid a second clutch, and chicks Sandy and Luna hatched in early April. Now approaching fledging age—when they'll take their first flights at 10 to 14 weeks—the eaglets face a gauntlet of dangers: hawks, owls, inclement weather, and especially cars when scavenging roadkill. Only about 70% of fledglings survive. The eagle family's saga has captivated millions via the 24/7 livestream. In 2025, a March snowstorm killed one of three chicks; the survivors, Sunny and Gizmo, successfully fledged. Jackie and Shadow have beaten the odds before—only half of eagle eggs hatch—and their resilience embodies the precarious beauty of wild parenthood. As Sandy and Luna flap their wings and practice squirrel-shooing of their own, the livestream continues to offer an unfiltered window into nature's triumphs and heartbreaks.
why_it_matters: The Big Bear eagle cam gives millions a raw, unedited look at wild parenthood—showing both fierce defense and fragile survival. It connects viewers to conservation in a visceral way, turning a slapstick squirrel encounter into a lesson about the real odds faced by species we have brought back from the brink.

background_read: Bald eagles were once endangered in the United States, with fewer than 500 nesting pairs in the lower 48 states by the 1960s due to habitat loss, hunting, and DDT poisoning. Legal protection and conservation efforts have brought them back to over 70,000 pairs today, and nest cams like the Big Bear Lake livestream have played a key role in building public support for wildlife.

The San Bernardino flying squirrel (a subspecies of Humboldt's flying squirrel) is a nocturnal glider found in Southern California mountains. Unlike the eagles, these squirrels do not truly fly; they use a membrane stretched between their legs to glide between trees, sometimes covering 300 feet.

Friends of Big Bear Valley (FOBBV) is a nonprofit that installed the eagle nest camera in 2015. The 24/7 stream has documented multiple nesting seasons, including tragedies like the 2025 snowstorm that killed one of three chicks, and triumphs like Sunny and Gizmo fledging successfully.

Fledging is a critical period: young eagles must build strength and learn to hunt while avoiding predators, collisions, and human-made hazards. Only about 70% survive their first year. Jackie and Shadow have nested for over a decade, becoming well-known figures in the local ecosystem.

perspectives.description: The bald eagle's recovery from near-extinction is a testament to effective environmental laws and public support. Livestreams like this one build empathy and donations, helping fund further habitat protection.

Some biologists worry that constant, close-up filming can disturb wildlife or make people intervene inappropriately when they witness natural mortality. The eagles may be accustomed to the camera, but the squirrel's visit shows the nest is never truly private.

These livestreams provide a wealth of behavioral data that would be hard to collect otherwise. The interaction between eagles and flying squirrels, rarely documented, helps researchers understand nest ecology and interspecies relationships.

As Big Bear Lake sees more development and climate shifts alter prey availability, future nesting seasons may become harder. Monitoring over many years will show whether these eagles can adapt, and what additional protections they might need.
